It began in the first week of January, when the wind swung round to the north and stayed there. Each morning the ice was thicker: first as thin as glass, then as thick as a loaf, then so thick that a grown man could jump on it and not hear a creak. The narrowboats were stuck fast at the wharf, still loaded with sacks of flour from the mill. Every week those boats carried the flour sixteen kilometres to the market at Kingsford, where the town's six bakers turned it into bread. Now nothing could move. The miller laughed at first, then stopped laughing and fetched it. Down at the wharf the boatmen tied twenty sacks of flour to it with ropes, while their wives filled flasks with hot tea. writing.summary-point k=0,r=2,t=On a windy day the rope bridge sways like a hammock, and first-time walkers grip both ropes. It was built a hundred years ago from hemp rope and oak planks, by people from the villages on both sides of the gorge. Before it, the only way across was a day's walk round the head of the gorge, so the two villages hardly met. Each had its own school, its own market and its own band, and each thought the other rather odd. The bridge changed that within a few years. Children from the far side began crossing to the bigger school, and families crossed back on market day. Today the two villages share one school, one market and one band, and many families have a grandparent on each side. The planks are replaced every spring, and a keeper checks the ropes each morning. People still argue about which side the bridge belongs to, but most agree that it made two villages into one.,title=The rope bridge,right=People still argue about which side...,w1=On a windy day the rope bridge sways...,w2=The planks are replaced every spring...

writing.summary-point k=1,r=2,t=Ferns grow from the walls of the mill by the falls, and a rowan tree leans over its door. For more than a hundred years, though, it was the busiest building in the gorge. Water from the falls turned its wheel, the wheel turned two millstones, and the stones ground wheat into flour for three villages. Farmers brought their wheat by cart, and the miller took one sack in every ten as his pay. Then, in 1890, the railway reached the valley, and trains brought cheap flour from great mills in the city. Within ten years the farmers stopped bringing wheat, and the mill fell silent. So the mill did not wear out: it was the railway, not the river or the years, that closed it. Its roof fell in during a storm in 1931. Last year the village mended the wheel, and on Saturdays the stones turn again.,title=The mill,right=So the mill did not wear out...,w1=Ferns grow from the walls of the mill...,w2=Farmers brought their wheat by cart...
